description: We’re a team of Polytechnique Montréal students with a shared fascination for space and a bias toward building. We combine engineering, software, and a lot of curiosity to tackle one question: what will it take for humans to actually live in space habitats? We’re turning one piece of that answer into a working project.
summary:
AstroWrap is a web app that finds terrestrial analogs for any site on the Moon or Mars. You choose a mission type and paint an area on a 3D globe of the Moon or Mars. AstroWrap reads that area’s profile across several criteria: relief and slopes, temperature and light extremes, wind, ice and water, caves and lava tubes, and rock types. It then searches the whole Earth for the closest match. A visible funnel removes the regions that don’t fit, one criterion at a time, and ranks the best candidates. For each site it shows real values next to the reference area, a 3D terrain comparison and a shareable “Wrap” recap.

This answers the challenge by finding new analog sites quickly and in a way you can explain, not only the famous ones. A “Responsible testing” mode estimates the CO₂ of travelling to each site and flags protected areas. It matters because testing rovers, habitats and crews in the right place on Earth makes missions safer and cheaper, without damaging our own planet.
details:
AstroWrap: find the place on Earth that looks most like your spot on the Moon or Mars

What it does. AstroWrap helps mission planners, scientists and students find terrestrial analogs: places on Earth that look like a chosen site on the Moon or Mars. You start on a 3D globe of the Moon or Mars, pick a mission type (balanced, landing, geology, astrobiology or climate) and paint any area with a brush. You aren’t limited to known landing sites. AstroWrap reads that area’s profile across several modules: relief and slopes, temperature and light extremes, wind and atmosphere, ice and water, caves and lava tubes, and rock types. It then compares the area with every Earth cell of the same size.

The search works as a funnel you can watch. Satellites scan your area, one per module. Each criterion then removes the Earth regions that don’t match, and the best candidates are ranked. For each site you see real values next to the reference area, not abstract scores, plus a 2D/3D view comparing the terrain. A “Wrap” recap, inspired by Spotify Wrapped, sums up the result in a few cards.

Benefits and impact. Testing rovers, habitats, instruments and astronauts on Earth is much cheaper and safer than learning on site. AstroWrap turns a manual expert search into a quick, explainable comparison, so teams can find new analog sites, not only the famous ones. Our “Responsible testing” mode adds the human side. It estimates the CO₂ of travelling to each site (UK DESNZ 2025 factors), flags protected areas (WDPA) and can re-rank the sites by environmental cost. The goal is to explore space without damaging Earth.

Tools. Python preprocessing pipeline over NASA and planetary datasets, the Mars Climate Database and Earth datasets. Everything is indexed on Uber’s H3 hexagonal grid and stored as Parquet. A FastAPI + DuckDB server does the scoring. The web client is plain JavaScript, with MapLibre for Earth, and globe.gl/three.js for the Moon, Mars and the 3D terrain. It’s hosted at astrowrap.earth, on GitHub and the cloud.

Creativity. You can paint any area instead of choosing from a fixed list. The funnel is visible and you can control it. The satellite animation shows each module at work. And we turned planetary science into a shareable “Wrap” story.

What we considered. We made each criterion removable and weighted it by mission type, because a landing site and an astrobiology site need different things. We kept results explainable, with real units and Earth reference values. Data licences mattered too: raw Mars Climate Database and WDPA data stay off the public app, and only derived values are shown, with citations. Speed on a small server and ease of use for non-experts were the other factors.
